    Age 8 — Age of Baoth

    The Prosperous Beginning¶

    In its early centuries, Baoth was a genuinely prosperous era. Trade flourished under the dragon dynasty's protection. The bureaucracy — while vast — was functional. Roads were built. Cities grew. The standard of living rose.

    Goldenborn ruled from the Obsidian Throne in the heart of Baoth. His court was a marvel of multi-species governance — humans, elves, dwarves, catmen, all serving in the imperial administration. The dragon's justice was swift and impartial. Merchants traveled the empire's roads without fear of bandits. The Baothian mark became the standard currency across Erisdar.

    The Shadows, operating from beneath Pontus, saw Baoth as their masterpiece in progress. Phase 3 of their plan was to transform Baoth into a pan-continental super-state — the vehicle through which they would eventually unify all of Ge'or under a single centralized authority. They embedded homunculi agents throughout the imperial administration: Councilor Varik, the emperor's chief advisor; Marshal Korr, commander of the northern legions; High Scribe Elara, who controlled the flow of information to the throne. They possessed Goldenborn himself — subtly at first, then completely.

    For a time, it worked.

    The Surveillance State¶

    The prosperity did not last. Under Shadow influence, Baoth transformed from an empire into a surveillance system. The bureaucracy became a machine of control:

    • Every citizen was registered at birth. Name, species, parentage, residence. The Imperial Census was updated annually — an administrative feat no previous empire had achieved.
    • Every transaction was recorded. The Baothian tax system tracked every coin that changed hands. Merchants who under-reported were disappeared. The empire's ledgers were the most comprehensive accounting in Ge'orian history.
    • Every dissent was noted. The Office of Imperial Harmony employed informants in every district. Citizens who criticized the emperor were visited by agents of the Office. Some were fined. Some were re-educated. Some were never seen again.
    • The empire centralized relentlessly — stripping power from regional lords, eliminating the countism that had characterized earlier ages. Local castles were demolished or converted into imperial garrisons. Regional currencies were banned. All roads led to Baoth, and all decisions came from Baoth.
    • Poverty struck. The surveillance state was expensive. The costs fell on the common people — higher taxes, mandatory labor for imperial projects, confiscation of property from those deemed insufficiently loyal. The dragon emperor — isolated in his palace, manipulated, fed false reports by Varik and Elara — had no clue. They told him the empire was thriving, that poverty was a temporary adjustment, that the dissenters were a tiny minority of malcontents. He believed them.

    Day to Day Under Surveillance¶

    For the average citizen of late-era Baoth, life was a sequence of checkpoints. Every morning: report to the district registrar. Every purchase: recorded in the imperial ledger. Every conversation in a public square: potentially monitored. The Office of Imperial Harmony employed over 200,000 informants across the empire — roughly one for every fifty citizens.

    Citizens developed coping mechanisms. They spoke in code. They gathered in private homes rather than public squares. They taught their children to smile at the registrar and say nothing of substance at the market. An entire culture of learned deception emerged — people who appeared perfectly loyal on the surface while maintaining entirely separate private lives. The Shadows, ironically, had created a population of expert liars.

    The dragon emperor was not evil. He was a puppet. The strings were held by the Shadows, and he never saw them.

    The Demonic Invasion¶

    The age ended in fire.

    The Demon King, having spent 60 years studying a Hybrian tablet, discovered the truth. The Shadows were inside Baoth. They were using the empire as a stepping stone to global control. If they succeeded, the Last Great War would restart — and this time, there would be no Union of Sovereign Planets to stop it.

    Kirivis attacked without explanation. The Demonic War (466–421 BGD) lasted 45 years. Baoth, already weakened by internal decay, could not withstand the assault. The surveillance state, for all its sophistication, had neglected its military. Its legions were designed for internal control, not external defense.

    In 421 BGD, Kirivis stormed the dragon hall. He told Goldenborn the truth: the Shadows had accomplished the sacrifice ceremony. The war itself was the ritual. Every death fed them. Goldenborn was no longer necessary. Rulfred — a Shadow in human form, celebrated as a hero — revealed himself. Kirivis was beheaded. The crowd cheered.

    Then Nethra, Kirivis's adopted daughter, detonated the Gift from 3,000,000 Years in Rulfred's throne room. The explosion destroyed Baoth entirely, created the Leviathan Sea, and transformed Nethra into something new.

    The Age of Baoth was over.

    Legacy¶

    Baoth's legacy is contradictory:

    • The Golden Age — its early centuries were genuinely prosperous, a model of multi-species governance under dragon rule.
    • The Surveillance State — its later centuries were a preview of what the Shadows intend for all of Ge'or: total control disguised as order.
    • The Learned Deception — Baoth's citizens became expert liars to survive. This cultural trait persisted into later ages, making Erisdarians naturally resistant to centralized propaganda.
    • The Ruins — the Ruins of Baoth now lie at the center of the Leviathan Sea, surrounded by impassable forest. Inside is the Archive of the Traveler, containing the true history. It has never been opened.
    • The Lesson — Baoth proved that centralized power, no matter how prosperous its beginnings, can be corrupted from within. The Shadows' greatest weapon is not force. It is bureaucracy. And the greatest defense against it — as the Baothian survivors proved — is the refusal to be fully known.
